noteBlocks.lede: A plant leaks water all day long. It evaporates inside the leaf and drifts out through the stomata, and the pull that replaces it drags water all the way up from the roots. A potometer is how you measure it.

noteBlocks.text: Transpiration, the potometer and uses of water

noteBlocks.md: A sunflower drinks about a litre of water on a hot day, and almost none of it stays. It evaporates out of the leaves as invisible vapour. That steady leak has a name — transpiration — and it is what pulls water up from the roots.

noteBlocks.md:
**1. Evaporation** from the surfaces of the **mesophyll cells**.
**2. Diffusion through the air spaces** between the spongy cells.
**3. Out through the stomata**, because there is more vapour inside the leaf than outside.

What is lost is replaced by water pulled up the **xylem**, which is why transpiration and water uptake go together.

noteBlocks.explain: Stomata. Both the air spaces and the stomata are worth a mark of their own, so name them both.

noteBlocks.title: Why one idea explains all five
noteBlocks.md:
Vapour leaves because there is **more of it inside the leaf than outside**. Anything that makes that difference bigger speeds transpiration up; anything that makes it smaller slows it down.

Wind sweeps the vapour away, so the difference grows. Warmth makes more vapour inside, so the difference grows. Humid air is already full of vapour, so the difference shrinks — and that is why humidity is the odd one out.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which factor is the only one that makes the rate go DOWN as it increases?
noteBlocks.explain: Humidity. Damp air outside means a smaller difference in water vapour concentration, so the vapour diffuses out more slowly.

noteBlocks.md:
Every joint is **airtight** and the whole tube is full of water, so every cubic millimetre the shoot takes up has to be drawn in at the open end — and the bubble is carried along with it. How far the bubble travels **is** how much water the shoot has taken up.

To **reset** it, open the **tap on the reservoir**: water runs in and pushes the bubble back to the start. Some potometers use a syringe, and you push the plunger.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which way does the bubble move while the shoot is taking up water?
noteBlocks.explain: Towards the shoot. The bubble follows the water being drawn in to replace what the leaves lost.

noteBlocks.title: Worked example: 'The bubble moved from 10 mm to 42 mm in 20 minutes. Calculate the rate. [2]'
noteBlocks.md:
**Step 1 — find the distance.** 42 − 10 = **32 mm**. The bubble did not start at zero, so the subtraction is a mark of its own.
**Step 2 — divide by the time.** 32 ÷ 20 = **1.6 mm per minute**. A rate is always an amount per unit of time, and the unit falls straight out of the division.

noteBlocks.prompt: Your turn for run C: the bubble went from 10 mm to 50 mm in 20 minutes. Give the rate in mm per minute.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "Transpiration"
noteBlocks.why: A short second pass over the same factors, now that you have the mechanism.

noteBlocks.md:
From run A to run B the rate rose from 1.6 to 2.4 mm per minute — an increase of 0.8. As a percentage of what you started with:

0.8 ÷ 1.6 × 100 = **50.0%**

And when a question says *use data to explain*, the figures themselves are the marks.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a percentage increase, what do you divide the increase by?
noteBlocks.explain: The original. Dividing by the new value is the commonest slip in this calculation, in every subject.

At midday the light is brightest and the air warmest, so the stomata are wide open for photosynthesis and the vapour leaves fast. Overnight the stomata close and uptake almost stops.

noteBlocks.md:
A **weight potometer** stands the whole apparatus on a balance: the mass lost is the water taken up, and a layer of oil stops anything evaporating from the flask. Ours fell from 186.50 g to 184.70 g in 30 minutes. The **washing-line method** weighs cut leaves, hangs them up and weighs them again.

The water a plant keeps has four uses: **support**, **transport**, **transpiration** and **photosynthesis**.

noteBlocks.explain: 186.50 − 184.70 = 1.80 g, which is the water the shoot took up.

steps.decision: The definition has three stages and CCEA wants all of them. Stage one is evaporation, inside the leaf, from the cell surfaces.

steps.working: …followed by diffusion of the water vapour through the air spaces…
steps.decision: Stage two. 'Air spaces' is a separate mark from 'stomata', and the 2025 reports say it is the one candidates leave out.
Stage three, the exit. Note the direction: water leaves here. It never enters the leaf this way.

steps.working: Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour.

steps.decision: The mark is for the smaller difference, not for the word humid. Every factor in this topic works through that same difference.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from the mesophyll cells, followed by diffusion of the water vapour through the air spaces and out through the stomata. In humid air there is already a lot of water vapour outside, so the difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces and the air outside is smaller and the vapour diffuses out more slowly.

twin.stem: State the two structures inside a leaf that water vapour passes through on its way out.

accepted: the air spaces and the stomata

items.stem: Before we start, three things you have already met. Which layer of a leaf carries out most gas exchange?

options.text: the spongy mesophyll
options.feedback: Its loose cells and large air spaces are the route in and out — and the same air spaces carry water vapour away.

options.text: the palisade mesophyll
options.feedback: The palisade layer is packed tight for light absorption. Gas exchange needs the spaces of the spongy layer.

options.text: the waxy cuticle
options.feedback: The cuticle is waterproof, which is the opposite of a gas-exchange surface.

options.text: the upper epidermis
options.feedback: A protective transparent layer with almost no stomata in it.

items.stem: What are the pores in the lower surface of a leaf called?

options.text: stomata
options.feedback: Stomata — the pores themselves. You will need this word in almost every answer in this topic.

options.text: guard cells
options.feedback: The guard cells open and close the pore. The pore is the stoma.

options.text: air spaces
options.feedback: The air spaces are inside the leaf, between the spongy cells. The pores in the surface are the stomata.

options.text: xylem vessels
options.feedback: Xylem vessels are the tubes that bring water up. They do not open onto the leaf surface.

options.text: out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one
options.feedback: Water goes where there is less of it. That is what pulls water out of the soil and into a root.

options.text: out of the concentrated solution and into the more dilute one
options.feedback: That is the way the sugar would go if it could fit through. Water moves the other way.

options.text: wherever the plant needs it most
options.feedback: Osmosis has no plan: it is diffusion, and it only ever runs down a difference in concentration.

options.text: the air into the leaf through the stomata
options.feedback: Water leaves a leaf through the stomata as vapour. It enters the plant at the roots.

items.stem: Water vapour leaves a leaf through…

options.text: the air spaces, then the stomata
options.feedback: Both structures, in that order. The scheme gives a mark for each, and the air spaces are the one most candidates leave out.

options.text: the stomata only
options.feedback: Half the answer. The vapour has to cross the air spaces inside the leaf first, and that is a mark of its own.

options.text: the xylem vessels
options.feedback: The xylem brings water up to the leaf; it does not carry vapour out of it.

options.text: the waxy cuticle
options.feedback: The cuticle is waterproof, which is exactly what stops water escaping through the upper surface.

items.stem: As light intensity increases, the rate of transpiration…
items.skill: State the direction of a factor's effect

options.text: increases, because the stomata open wider
options.feedback: Light opens the stomata for photosynthesis, and open stomata let more water vapour out.

options.text: decreases, because the stomata close
options.feedback: The stomata close in the dark, not in the light. Summer 2025 examiners reported candidates giving this relationship the wrong way round.

options.text: stays the same, because light is not a factor
options.feedback: Light intensity is one of the five factors named in the specification.

options.text: increases, because the plant makes more water in photosynthesis
options.feedback: Photosynthesis does make water, but the amount is tiny and irrelevant here. The link is through the stomata opening.

items.stem: Which way does the air bubble in a bubble potometer move, and why?
items.skill: Explain the movement of the bubble

options.text: Towards the shoot, because water is taken up to replace what is lost by transpiration
options.feedback: The bubble follows the water column. That is all it is measuring.

options.text: Away from the shoot, because water is pushed out of the leaves
options.feedback: Water leaves the leaf as vapour through the stomata, so water is drawn IN at the cut end and the bubble follows it towards the shoot.

options.text: Away from the shoot, because oxygen from photosynthesis pushes it along
options.feedback: The tube is full of water, not gas from the leaf. Summer 2025 examiners saw exactly this answer and it earned nothing.

options.text: Towards the shoot, because water enters the leaf through the stomata
options.feedback: The direction is right but the reason is not: water leaves through the stomata as vapour. It enters at the cut end of the stem.

items.stem: In run A the bubble moved from 10 mm to 42 mm in 20 minutes. What was the rate of water uptake?
items.skill: Calculate a rate from two readings

options.text: 1.6 mm per minute
options.feedback: Distance 32 mm divided by 20 minutes.

options.text: 2.10 mm per minute
options.feedback: The final reading has been divided by the time without subtracting the start. The bubble began at a mark, not at zero.

options.text: 32 mm per minute
options.feedback: That is the distance the bubble moved, not a rate. A rate needs dividing by the time.

options.text: 0.625 mm per minute
options.feedback: Time has been divided by distance. Rate is the amount first, the time second: distance ÷ time.

items.stem: How do you reset the air bubble to the start of the scale between runs?

options.text: Open the tap on the reservoir so water pushes the bubble back
options.feedback: The reservoir is there for exactly this. Some set-ups use a syringe instead of a tap, and pushing the plunger does the same job.

options.text: Blow down the capillary tube
options.feedback: That would add air and break the water column. Use the reservoir tap or the syringe.

options.text: Lift the shoot out and put it back
options.feedback: Breaking the seal lets air in, and the airtight seal is what makes the measurement mean anything.

options.text: Wait until it drifts back on its own
options.feedback: It will not: the shoot goes on taking water up, so the bubble only travels one way.

items.stem: Which change would make the rate of transpiration fall?
items.skill: Pick the factor that lowers the rate

options.text: Sealing the shoot inside a clear plastic bag
options.feedback: The bag traps water vapour, so the air around the leaves becomes humid and the vapour diffuses out more slowly.

options.text: Switching on a fan
options.feedback: Moving air carries vapour away, keeping the outside air drier, so the rate rises.

options.text: Moving the plant to a warmer room
options.feedback: Warmth gives the water molecules more energy, so evaporation and diffusion are faster and the rate rises.

options.text: Adding two more leaves to the shoot
options.feedback: More leaf surface area means more stomata, so the rate rises.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the uses of water the specification lists for a plant?

options.text: Breaking down glucose to release energy
options.feedback: That is respiration, and it uses oxygen, not water. The four listed uses are support, transport, transpiration and photosynthesis.

options.text: Keeping the cells turgid so the plant is supported
options.feedback: Support is one of the four uses: turgid cells hold a soft plant upright.

options.text: Carrying dissolved minerals around the plant
options.feedback: Transport is one of the four uses.

options.text: Supplying a raw material for photosynthesis
options.feedback: Photosynthesis is one of the four uses: water is one of the two reactants.

parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate at which water was taken up between run A and run B. Give your answer to one decimal place.

scheme.for: rates are 1.6 and 2.4 mm per minute
increase = 0.8 mm per minute

hints: Rates first, then the increase, then divide by the original rate.
parts.workedSolution: Run A: 32 ÷ 20 = 1.6 mm per minute. Run B: 48 ÷ 20 = 2.4 mm per minute. Increase = 0.8 mm per minute, and 0.8 ÷ 1.6 × 100 = 50.0%.

parts.stem: State what happens to the rate of transpiration when the air around a leaf becomes more humid.

scheme.for: it decreases / slows down

parts.workedSolution: It decreases.

commonErrors.feedback: Humidity is the one factor that slows transpiration down. Summer 2025 examiners recorded candidates giving the relationship the wrong way round.

parts.stem: Explain your answer to part (a).

accepted: humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so the difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces and the air outside is smaller and the vapour diffuses out more slowly

scheme.for: humid air already contains a lot of water vapour
so the difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces and the outside air is smaller, and diffusion out is slower

hints: Compare the air inside the leaf with the air outside.
parts.workedSolution: Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour. The difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces inside the leaf and the air outside is therefore smaller, so the vapour diffuses out through the stomata more slowly.

parts.stem: Water keeps a plant's cells turgid. State the use of water this describes.

scheme.for: support

parts.workedSolution: Support.

parts.stem: Water is one of the two raw materials the plant combines in the chloroplasts. State the use of water this describes.

scheme.for: photosynthesis

parts.workedSolution: Photosynthesis.

parts.stem: A shoot stands in a flask of water on a balance. The water surface is covered with a layer of oil. The whole apparatus weighed 186.50 g at the start and 184.70 g after 30 minutes. Calculate the mass of water lost.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass of the whole apparatus at the end. The water lost is the difference between the two weighings.

parts.stem: Suggest why a layer of oil is poured on the water surface in the flask.

accepted: to stop water evaporating from the surface of the flask, so the only mass lost is the water the shoot took up

scheme.for: to stop water evaporating from the surface, so the mass lost is only the water taken up by the shoot

hints: What else could take mass off the balance?
parts.workedSolution: The oil stops water evaporating from the open surface of the flask. Without it, some of the mass lost would have nothing to do with the shoot, and the reading would be too high.

parts.stem: Calculate the mass of water the shoot took up in one minute. Give your answer in grams, to two decimal places.
hints: Divide the mass lost by the number of minutes.
parts.workedSolution: 1.80 ÷ 30 = 0.06 g in one minute.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass lost over the whole 30 minutes. Divide it by 30 to get the mass in one minute.

context.setting: Cut leaves hung on a line and reweighed the next day

parts.stem: Four cut leaves were hung on a line in a warm room. Together they weighed 12.50 g at the start and 8.75 g after 24 hours. Calculate the percentage of their mass that was lost. Give your answer to one decimal place.
hints: Mass lost first, then divide by the mass at the start.
parts.workedSolution: Mass lost = 12.50 − 8.75 = 3.75 g. As a percentage of the starting mass: 3.75 ÷ 12.50 × 100 = 30.0%.

parts.stem: Explain why the leaves lost mass.

accepted: water evaporated from the mesophyll cells and the vapour diffused out through the stomata, and nothing replaced it because the leaves were cut off the plant

scheme.for: water was lost by transpiration through the stomata
and it was not replaced, because the leaves were cut from the plant

hints: Where did the water go, and why did none arrive to replace it?
parts.workedSolution: Water evaporated from the mesophyll cells and the vapour diffused out through the stomata. Because the leaves had been cut from the plant there was no water coming up the xylem to replace it, so the mass of the leaves fell.

data for temperature: 32 mm rises only to 40 mm, an increase of 8 mm

parts.stem: Name the two structures water vapour passes through as it leaves a leaf. Give the one inside the leaf first.

accepted: the air spaces and then the stomata

scheme.for: air spaces
stomata
scheme.examinerNote: Either order is credited on the real paper; both structures are needed for two marks.

hints: Two structures, two marks.
parts.workedSolution: The air spaces inside the leaf, and then the stomata.

commonErrors.feedback: Stomata alone is one mark of the two. The air spaces are the structure Summer 2025's candidates left out most often.

parts.stem: State which way the air bubble moves while the shoot is taking up water.

scheme.for: towards the shoot (to the right on this diagram)

parts.workedSolution: Towards the shoot.

parts.stem: Explain why the bubble moves in that direction.

accepted: water is lost from the leaves as vapour through the stomata, that water is replaced by water drawn up from the cut end of the shoot, and the bubble follows the water along the capillary tube

scheme.for: water is lost from the leaves as vapour (through the stomata)
that water is replaced by water drawn up from the cut end of the shoot
so water moves along the capillary tube and the bubble follows it

hints: Start where the water is lost, then say what replaces it.
parts.workedSolution: Water evaporates from the mesophyll cells and the vapour diffuses out through the stomata. That lost water is replaced by water drawn up from the cut end of the shoot, so water moves along the capillary tube towards the shoot and the air bubble is carried along with it.

commonErrors.feedback: The tube is full of water, and nothing in it comes from photosynthesis. The bubble simply follows the water the shoot is taking up.
Water leaves the leaf through the stomata as vapour; it enters at the cut end of the stem. Summer 2025 examiners saw this exact reversal.

parts.stem: Calculate the rate of water uptake, in mm per minute, if the bubble moves from the 10 mm mark to the 42 mm mark in 20 minutes.

scheme.for: distance = 42 − 10 = 32 mm
32 ÷ 20 = 1.6 (mm per minute)

hints: Distance first, then divide by the time.
parts.workedSolution: Distance moved = 42 − 10 = 32 mm, so the rate is 32 ÷ 20 = 1.6 mm per minute.

commonErrors.feedback: The end reading has been divided by the time. Subtract the starting reading first: the bubble did not start at zero.
That is the distance the bubble moved, in mm. The question asks for mm per minute, so divide by the time.

context.setting: Four potometer runs on the same shoot

data.caption: The same shoot in four sets of conditions, 20 minutes each
rows: still air, 20 °C, shoot inside a sealed clear bag

parts.stem: Calculate the rate of water uptake in run D, in mm per minute.

scheme.for: 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6 (mm per minute)

parts.workedSolution: 22 − 10 = 12 mm, and 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6 mm per minute.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the distance moved. Divide it by the time to get a rate.

parts.stem: Explain why the rate in run D is lower than the rate in run A.

accepted: the bag traps the water vapour, so the air around the leaves becomes humid, the difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces and the air outside is smaller, and the vapour diffuses out more slowly

scheme.for: the bag traps the water vapour, so the air round the leaves becomes humid
the difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces and the outside air is smaller
so the vapour diffuses out of the stomata more slowly and less water is taken up

hints: What does the bag do to the air around the leaves?
Then compare inside the leaf with outside it.
parts.workedSolution: The sealed bag traps the water vapour leaving the leaves, so the air around them becomes humid. The difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces inside the leaf and the air just outside it is therefore smaller, so the vapour diffuses out through the stomata more slowly and the shoot takes up less water.

commonErrors.feedback: The first mark is for saying that the bag makes the air humid. Without that, the rest of the chain has nothing to hang on.

parts.stem: Use the table to work out the percentage increase in the rate of water uptake between run A and run C. Give your answer to one decimal place.

scheme.for: rates 1.6 and 2.0 mm per minute
increase = 0.4 mm per minute

hints: Divide by the rate you started from.
parts.workedSolution: The rates are 1.6 and 2.0 mm per minute, an increase of 0.4 mm per minute. As a percentage of the original rate: 0.4 ÷ 1.6 × 100 = 25.0%.

parts.stem: Use the graph to state the time of day at which water uptake was greatest. Give your answer as a time.

scheme.for: 12:00 / midday
scheme.examinerNote: Both midnight and midday appear on this axis, so the answer has to say which.

hints: Both midnight and midday are printed on the axis, so be exact.
parts.workedSolution: The peak is at 12:00, which is midday.

commonErrors.feedback: Midnight is where the line is lowest. Summer 2023 examiners warned that both midnight and midday appear on this axis, so the answer has to name the right one.

parts.stem: Use the graph to calculate how much greater the uptake was at that time than at 6:00. Give your answer in cm³ per hour.

scheme.for: readings 4.2 and 1.0 cm³ per hour
4.2 − 1.0 = 3.2 (cm³ per hour)

hints: Read both values off the graph before subtracting.
parts.workedSolution: At midday the uptake is 4.2 cm³ per hour and at 6:00 it is 1.0 cm³ per hour, so the difference is 3.2 cm³ per hour.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reading at midday on its own. The question asks how much greater it was, so subtract the earlier reading.

parts.stem: Explain why water uptake is greatest at that time of day.

accepted: light intensity and temperature are highest then, so the stomata are open for photosynthesis and the water evaporates and diffuses out faster, so more water has to be taken up to replace it

scheme.for: light intensity and temperature are at their highest around midday
so the stomata are open for photosynthesis and the water evaporates and diffuses out faster
more water is lost by transpiration, so more has to be taken up to replace it

hints: Two conditions are at their highest. What do they do to the stomata?
Finish by linking the loss to the uptake.
parts.workedSolution: Around midday the light intensity and the temperature are at their highest. The stomata are open for photosynthesis, and the warmth makes the water evaporate from the mesophyll cells and diffuse out through them faster. More water is therefore lost by transpiration, and the plant has to take up more water to replace it.

commonErrors.feedback: Light and heat are one mark of the three. Summer 2023 examiners recorded that only the more able candidates linked the peak to the stomata being open.

context.setting: A pot plant left unwatered on a sunny windowsill for a week

parts.stem: State two of the four uses a plant makes of the water it takes up, apart from transport and transpiration.

scheme.for: support
photosynthesis

hints: The specification names four uses in total.
parts.workedSolution: Support and photosynthesis.

commonErrors.feedback: Respiration releases water rather than using it. The four uses on this specification are support, transport, transpiration and photosynthesis.

parts.stem: The plant is left unwatered for a week and its leaves droop. Explain why.

accepted: the plant goes on losing water by transpiration but none is taken up to replace it, so the cells lose water and become flaccid, and flaccid cells no longer support the leaves

scheme.for: water goes on being lost from the leaves by transpiration
but there is no water in the soil to replace it
so the cells lose water and become flaccid, and flaccid cells no longer support the leaf

hints: Losses continue. What has stopped?
Finish on the word that describes a cell that has lost its water.
parts.workedSolution: Water goes on evaporating from the mesophyll cells and diffusing out through the stomata, so the plant keeps losing water by transpiration. With dry soil there is no water to take up to replace it, so the cells lose water and become flaccid. Flaccid cells no longer press against their walls, so they cannot hold the leaves up and the plant droops.

commonErrors.feedback: A drooping plant has flaccid cells, not turgid ones. Turgid is the state that holds a soft plant up.

parts.stem:
A student is given a bubble potometer, a leafy shoot, a stopwatch, a thermometer and three rooms kept at different temperatures.
Describe how she should use the potometer to find out how temperature affects the rate of water uptake by the shoot.
The quality of your written communication is marked here too, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; everything set out in a clear and sensible order; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; an order you can follow, though it is not held right through; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; ideas in an order that is hard to follow; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave what you meant unclear.

indicativeContent.point: cut the shoot and set it into the bung under water, so no air enters the tube
let an air bubble into the end of the capillary tube and note its starting position on the scale
measure the temperature of the room with the thermometer
time a fixed period with the stopwatch and record how far the bubble moves
reset the bubble with the reservoir tap (or the syringe) before the next run
repeat at each temperature, keeping the same shoot, the same time and the still air the same
calculate the rate as distance moved divided by time, and compare the rates

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Answers that describe the apparatus without saying what is measured, or that change more than one variable, cap at Band B. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Set up, measure, reset, repeat, calculate — one sentence each.
Two of the seven points are about keeping everything except the temperature the same.
parts.workedSolution: Cut the shoot and fit it into the rubber bung under water, so that no air gets into the tube, and check that the seal is airtight. Lift the open end of the capillary tube out of the beaker for a moment to let an air bubble in, then put it back and note the position of the bubble on the millimetre scale. Measure the temperature of the room with the thermometer. Start the stopwatch and, after a fixed time such as 20 minutes, record the new position of the bubble and work out the distance it has moved. Open the reservoir tap to push the bubble back to the start, then move the apparatus to the next room and repeat, using the same shoot, the same length of time and still air each time so that temperature is the only variable changed. Finally calculate the rate for each temperature as the distance moved divided by the time, and compare the rates.

commonErrors.feedback: Resetting the bubble is one of the indicative points, and it is the one Summer 2024's examiners said fewest candidates could describe. Name the reservoir tap or the syringe.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'The bubble moved from the 10 mm mark to the 42 mm mark in 20 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute. [2]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The bubble did not start at zero: it started at the 10 mm mark. 42 mm is where it finished, not how far it went, so line 1 should read 42 − 10 = 32 mm.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the two: dividing by the time is the right method, so the second mark survives on follow-through. The first mark goes with the distance. In the exam, write the subtraction on its own line before you divide — it takes three seconds and it is the step the scheme is looking for.

findTheMistake.stem:
Conall is asked: 'Explain why the air bubble in a potometer moves towards the shoot. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The leaves are photosynthesising in the light.
This makes oxygen, which pushes the bubble along the tube.
So the bubble moves towards the shoot.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The tube is full of water, not gas from the leaf, and the oxygen made in photosynthesis leaves through the stomata. What moves the bubble is the water the shoot takes up to replace the water it has lost as vapour.
correction: Water evaporates from the mesophyll cells and the vapour diffuses out through the stomata.
That water is replaced by water drawn up from the cut end of the shoot.
So water moves along the capillary tube and the bubble follows it towards the shoot.
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing here yet, though the direction in line 3 is right and on the real paper it would earn its own mark in a part that asks for the direction. Summer 2025's examiners reported exactly this answer: candidates treating the potometer as though it measured photosynthesis. The word to start with is transpiration, and the word that earns the last mark is replaced.

findTheMistake.stem:
Erin is asked: 'Describe what happens to the rate of transpiration as light intensity increases. [1]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: As the light intensity increases, the rate of transpiration decreases.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The relationship is the other way round. Light makes the stomata open for photosynthesis, and open stomata let more water vapour out, so brighter light means a faster rate of transpiration.
correction: As the light intensity increases, the rate of transpiration increases.
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing, because a relationship stated backwards is a different claim. Summer 2025's examiners flagged this on both tiers: the words were there but in the wrong order. Humidity is the only factor in this topic that lowers the rate — check which one you are being asked about before you write increases or decreases.

prompts.answer: The evaporation of water from the mesophyll cells, followed by diffusion of the water vapour through the air spaces and out through the stomata.

prompts.prompt: Name the two structures water vapour passes through as it leaves a leaf.
prompts.answer: The air spaces inside the leaf, and the stomata.

prompts.prompt: List the five factors that affect the rate of transpiration, and say which one lowers it.
prompts.answer: Surface area, wind, temperature, light intensity and humidity. Humidity is the one that lowers the rate.

prompts.prompt: As light intensity increases, what happens to the rate of transpiration, and why?
prompts.answer: It increases, because the stomata open for photosynthesis and open stomata let more water vapour out.

prompts.prompt: Why does humidity lower the rate of transpiration?
prompts.answer: Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so the difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces and the air outside is smaller and the vapour diffuses out more slowly.

prompts.prompt: How is the air bubble in a bubble potometer reset to the start of the scale?
prompts.answer: Open the tap on the reservoir, or push in the syringe plunger, so water pushes the bubble back.

prompts.prompt: Which way does the potometer bubble move, and why?
prompts.answer: Towards the shoot: water lost as vapour through the stomata is replaced by water drawn up from the cut end, and the bubble follows the water.

prompts.prompt: How do you turn a bubble's movement into a rate?
prompts.answer: Subtract the starting reading from the final reading to get the distance moved, then divide by the time taken.

prompts.prompt: Name the four uses a plant makes of water.
Why does a cut flower in a vase last longer in a cool, still room than on a sunny windowsill?
prompts.answer: Cool, still air lowers the rate of transpiration, so the flower loses water more slowly than it can take it up and its cells stay turgid.

prompts.prompt: Describe the washing-line method for investigating water loss from leaves.
prompts.answer: Weigh cut leaves, hang them up in the conditions being tested, reweigh them after a set time, and work out the mass lost.

prompts.prompt: Why is a layer of oil floated on the water in a weight potometer?
prompts.answer: To stop water evaporating from the open surface, so the mass lost is only the water the shoot took up.

findings.asked: Name the potometer, say how to reset the bubble, read and calculate its movement, then use data on two factors.
findings.wentWrong: Naming and calculating went well; fewer could reset the bubble; temperature was identified as the factor but the link to a faster rate of transpiration was often missing, and only the more able backed the choice with figures from the data.
findings.rule: Reset from the reservoir; a factor answer needs the factor, the direction of its effect on transpiration and the data that shows it.

findings.asked: Where water vapour leaves a leaf, how light intensity affects transpiration, and why the potometer bubble moves.
findings.wentWrong: Few could name stomata and air spaces; some stated the light-transpiration relationship the wrong way round; the bubble's direction earned a mark but explanations were confused - water thought to enter through the stomata, or the whole thing treated as oxygen from photosynthesis.
findings.rule: Water is pulled up to replace water lost as vapour through the stomata; the bubble follows the water towards the leaf.

findings.asked: Same paper at Higher: exit route, light intensity, another factor, and the bubble.
findings.wentWrong: Stomata was known but air spaces often missed; the same reversed relationship and the same two wrong explanations of the bubble appeared.
findings.rule: Say both: through the air spaces and out of the stomata.

findings.asked: A day-long graph of water uptake: read times, explain the peak, and what the stomata do.
findings.wentWrong: Times had to be exact (midday and midnight both appear on the axis); most said light or temperature was highest and photosynthesis was happening, but only the more able linked the peak to carbon dioxide entering through open stomata and to transpiration.
findings.rule: Read the axis precisely, then connect the peak to stomata being open for photosynthesis.

insight.ruleToRemember: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaf through the stomata (via the air spaces); water is pulled up the xylem to replace it, which is what moves the potometer bubble towards the plant. Rate rises with light, temperature and wind and falls with humidity; reset the bubble from the reservoir.
insight.aStarSignal: Reading a potometer or day-cycle graph and explaining the numbers with the mechanism - stomata open, vapour lost, water pulled up - rather than restating the trend.
